title: Dynamics Are Learned, Not Told: Latent Geometry for Zero-Shot Control
one_liner: Instead of asking a robot to name physical properties to adapt its skills, the paper learns a smooth map of control spaces that automatically handles unseen dynamics shifts.
lead: When a robot learns to move, it works well for one specific environment. If that environment changes—a joint becomes looser, the wind picks up, a tool gets heavier—the learned skills fail. Usually, engineers fix this by identifying and encoding the new parameters (like mass, friction) into the model. This paper instead learns a geometric space of all possible dynamics, using smoothness as the key principle, so robots adapt to new worlds without being told what changed.

paras: A robot trained to walk works great in its original setting. But when the ground changes (wet, sandy, steep), or the robot itself shifts (battery dies, joint rusts), the walking skill dies too.

The standard fix: an engineer lists the physical things that changed (weight, friction, motor torque) and encodes them into the model before retraining. This rigid list breaks: what if the change is something you didn't anticipate, such as a structural crack in the leg? What if multiple things shift at once in a way the list never imagined?

callout.b: The problem: a closed list of parameters cannot capture all possible world changes.
callout.html: The paper learns a continuous smooth space of all possible dynamics instead, so adaptation happens automatically.

steps.text: Let the robot move in many different worlds and record what happened.
Train a neural network to watch a short trajectory and output a location on a smooth map.
Use a learning signal that makes nearby worlds output nearby locations on the map.
The encoder never sees parameter labels; it infers world identity purely from how the robot moves.
When a new dynamic appears, the encoder finds its location and the policy adapts without retraining.

paras: The paper changes the trajectory encoder—the neural network that watches the robot move and outputs a representation of the current world state. Instead of outputting a list of named numbers (parameters like mass and friction), it outputs a location on a smooth, continuous space where nearby worlds map to nearby points.

hidden.h2: Lipschitz smoothness: the hidden quantity that controls adaptation
hidden.name: Lipschitz smoothness of the encoder
paras: Lipschitz smoothness is a formal measure of how abruptly a function changes. A smooth function produces only gradual output shifts when the input changes slightly; a jagged function produces wild jumps. The paper proves mathematically that the robot's ability to adapt to new dynamics depends on how smooth the encoder is.

The paper estimates and controls this smoothness by using a specific learning signal—a multi-positive contrastive objective—that encourages the encoder to map similar trajectories close together and dissimilar ones far apart. This creates smoothness automatically without needing to label what properties differ.

heat.caption: Darker means more similar to the test trajectory. Bordered (similar pairs) train the smoothness.

reads.html: How much does the encoder's output move when the input changes a little? That is Lipschitz smoothness.
The Lipschitz constant upper-bounds adaptation error. Multi-positive InfoNCE optimizes this constant by pulling similar examples close on the learned geometric space.

mechanism.h2: Why smoothness solves the adaptation problem
paras: If two worlds are physically similar, a smooth encoder places them close together on the geometric space. The robot's policy, trained on many points in this space, naturally knows how to behave in the region between them. When the robot encounters a new world for the first time, the encoder places it somewhere on the space; the policy then uses nearby trained examples to guide its action, blending behaviors smoothly.

This is mathematically provable: the error the robot makes in a new world is bounded by how smooth the encoder is. A jagged encoder creates dead zones where no training data exists nearby—the policy must guess. A smooth encoder ensures that every plausible world lives in a well-trained neighborhood, so the policy can interpolate from nearby trained examples rather than extrapolating blind.

stages.s: Encoder finds its location on the smooth space
Policy blends them based on closeness

math.h2: The learning signal that builds smoothness
math.words: For each trajectory sample, pull all similar trajectories close on the map and push dissimilar ones far. The penalty is zero if similar pairs sit within a small distance and dissimilar pairs sit outside it.
math.equation: L = mean over positive pairs of max(0, distance - margin) + mean over negative pairs of max(0, margin - distance)
symbols: two trajectories from similar or same dynamics
how far apart the two encoded outputs sit
the target separation (e.g., 0.1 in encoding space)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Positive pair (similar worlds): distance = 0.05, margin = 0.1. Penalty = max(0, 0.05 - 0.1) = 0. Good.
Positive pair (similar worlds): distance = 0.15, margin = 0.1. Penalty = max(0, 0.15 - 0.1) = 0.05. Bad, pull closer.
Negative pair (different worlds): distance = 0.08, margin = 0.1. Penalty = max(0, 0.1 - 0.08) = 0.02. Bad, push apart.
Negative pair (different worlds): distance = 0.3, margin = 0.1. Penalty = max(0, 0.1 - 0.3) = 0. Good.

math.note: This loss creates a space where similar trajectories cluster close and dissimilar ones stay far apart, giving the encoder its smoothness.

bars.h2: Adaptation success on unseen dynamics shifts

charts.title: Old method: explicit parameter encoding
charts.note: Fails on unmodeled changes because the parameter list is rigid and incomplete.

charts.title: This paper: smooth geometry
charts.note: Succeeds on new shifts because the smooth space generalizes to any nearby world the policy has partially seen.

items.b: Covariate shift: if test worlds are far outside the training set.
items.html: If all training dynamics are mild (small changes in mass) but a test world has a severe structural failure, the encoder has never seen that region of the space. Even with smoothness, blending nearby examples fails when nothing in training is actually nearby.
If trajectories are short or repetitive, the encoder cannot distinguish between subtly different dynamics. The learned space becomes crumpled and loses smoothness where it matters most.

The margin parameter controls how tightly similar worlds cluster versus how spread out different ones are. If too tight, the space becomes crowded and new worlds have no room to interpolate cleanly. If too loose, the space becomes sparse and smoothness is lost.

items.b: Done right: train on diverse dynamics, use trajectories long enough to reveal dynamics clearly, and tune the margin by testing.
items.html: Validate smoothness on a held-out subset before deploying to new worlds.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple demo where a robot learns to reach a target in multiple physics engines (e.g., different friction, mass, damping in MuJoCo). Train the encoder on 20 random dynamics and freeze it. Then, on 5 new held-out dynamics the encoder never trained on, show that the policy adapts instantly and successfully. Measure success rate as the fraction of new dynamics where the robot reaches the target within 50 timesteps.
demo.metric_eq: adaptation success = (# new dynamics where target reached) / (# new dynamics tested)
demo.closing: The demo must show that zero-shot adaptation to unseen worlds works because the smooth space lets the policy interpolate from nearby training examples rather than guess blind.
